interventions.name: Legume-based cover cropping
interventions.mechanism: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through symbiotic rhizobia bacteria, contributing 50–200 kg N/ha/year. Continuous root biomass from cover crops feeds soil microbial communities, increasing microbial biomass carbon by 15–25% within 2–3 cropping cycles. Flowering legumes also provide nectar and pollen resources for pollinating insects during periods when cash crops are not in bloom.
interventions.effect_size: +15–25% soil organic carbon over 2–3 years; 50–200 kg N/ha/year biological nitrogen fixation
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Technical Summary (2022) & FAO Soil Organic Carbon (Poeplau & Don, 2015)
co_benefits: Reduced synthetic nitrogen fertilizer costs
Suppression of weed emergence during fallow periods
Enhanced wild pollinator foraging habitat
trade_offs: Initial seed and establishment expenditure
Soil moisture consumption in moisture-critical planting windows

interventions.name: Agroforestry and intercropping in semi-arid monoculture systems
interventions.mechanism: Tree and shrub layers reduce wind erosion by up to 50% and lower soil surface temperatures by 2–5°C, decreasing evapotranspiration and improving effective water-use efficiency. Leaf litter inputs add carbon to soil, while vertical habitat structure (canopy, understorey, ground layer) creates microhabitat niches absent in open monocultures, supporting 30–50% higher arthropod diversity.
interventions.effect_size: 2–9 tonnes C/ha/year sequestration; 30–50% higher arthropod diversity; measurable increases in canopy-dependent species richness within 3–5 years
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia (Section 10.4) & Nair et al. (2009)
co_benefits: Diversified revenue streams from timber, fruit, and fodder
Microclimate buffering against extreme heat waves
Groundwater recharge enhancement
trade_offs: Competition for sunlight and moisture with cash crops if canopy unmanaged
Increased labor requirements for pruning and harvesting

interventions.name: Riparian buffer strip establishment
interventions.mechanism: Vegetated strips of 10–30 m width along waterways filter agricultural runoff through physical trapping, root uptake, and microbial denitrification, removing 85–95% of sediment and 50–85% of nitrogen. The strips function as ecological corridors connecting fragmented habitat patches, enabling species dispersal across agricultural landscapes and supporting 2–3× higher plant species density than adjacent farmland.
interventions.effect_size: 85–95% sediment removal; 50–85% nitrogen removal; 2–3× plant species richness per unit area
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Cross-Chapter Paper 1 (CCP1: Biodiversity Hotspots) & Mayer et al. (2007)
co_benefits: Protection against bank erosion and flood damage
Thermal buffering of aquatic habitats
Recreational and aesthetic landscape value
trade_offs: Loss of productive cropland area along waterways
Potential habitat for localized wildlife grazing

interventions.name: Hedgerow and field margin floral restoration
interventions.mechanism: Native hedgerow species (hawthorn, blackthorn, elder, dog rose) extend the flowering season from March through October, providing continuous nectar and pollen when crop flowers are absent. Structurally diverse margins harbour populations of natural pest enemies (hoverflies, parasitoid wasps, ground beetles) that spill over into adjacent crops, reducing aphid populations by 30–50%.
interventions.effect_size: 25–50% higher pollinator abundance; 30% greater pollinator species richness; 40–60% increase in natural pest control services within 2–3 years
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & IPBES Pollinators Assessment (Holland et al., 2016)
co_benefits: Biological pest regulation saving chemical spray costs
Windbreak protection reducing crop lodging
Connectivity for small mammals and songbirds
trade_offs: Requires periodic mechanical trimming and maintenance
Minor field area taken out of primary crop production

interventions.name: Holistic planned rotational grazing
interventions.mechanism: Systematic paddock rotation with periodic rest intervals allows grasses to regrow deep root systems that deposit carbon at depth, improving soil structure and increasing SOC. Grazing pressure management maintains plant species diversity by preventing competitive exclusion, while hoof action breaks soil crusts in semi-arid systems, improving water infiltration and seed-soil contact.
interventions.effect_size: +0.5–1.0 tonnes C/ha/year in top 30 cm; 20–40% increase in pasture plant species richness; vegetation cover recovery from <30% to >70% within 3–5 years in degraded rangelands
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & Teague et al. (2011)
co_benefits: Higher livestock carrying capacity over time
Increased drought resilience of pastures
Even distribution of organic manure
trade_offs: Higher infrastructure capital for portable fencing and watering points
Requires intensive monitoring and dynamic paddock planning

interventions.name: Agricultural wetland and peatland re-wetting
interventions.mechanism: Restoring the water table in drained wetlands halts aerobic peat decomposition and associated carbon emissions, re-establishes anaerobic carbon accumulation, and restores hydrophytic vegetation communities. Rewetted areas rapidly recover aquatic invertebrate diversity, provide breeding habitat for waterfowl and amphibians, and function as natural water purification systems filtering agricultural nutrients.
interventions.effect_size: 0.5–2.0 tonnes C/ha/year re-accumulation; restoration of breeding habitat for waterfowl and amphibians within 5–10 years
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Cross-Chapter Paper 1 (CCP1: Biodiversity Hotspots) & Ramsar Convention (2018)
co_benefits: Regional flood risk mitigation and groundwater replenishment
Ecotourism and wildfowl habitat recovery
Major permanent carbon emission reduction
trade_offs: Permanent reduction of conventional agricultural output on rewetted land
Potential localized increase in initial methane emissions during stabilization

interventions.name: Conservation agriculture and reduced or no-tillage
interventions.mechanism: Eliminating or reducing tillage preserves soil aggregate structure and fungal hyphal networks (particularly arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi) critical for plant nutrient uptake and carbon stabilisation. Undisturbed soil surfaces maintain higher infiltration rates and develop a protective residue layer that reduces erosion. The shift to fungal-dominated microbial communities increases carbon-use efficiency and nutrient retention.
interventions.effect_size: +10–20% SOC in 0–10 cm layer over 5–10 years; 50–90% reduction in soil erosion; 20–50% increase in water infiltration; 30–60% higher AMF colonisation rates
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & Powlson et al. (2014)
co_benefits: Significant reduction in tractor fuel and labor expenses
Improved soil water infiltration during heavy downpours
Reduced particulate air pollution from field dust
trade_offs: Initial transition yield dip (1–3 years) during soil biology restructuring
Potential initial reliance on targeted herbicides for weed management

interventions.name: Permanent pollinator wildflower strips
interventions.mechanism: Narrow bands (3–6 m) of sown wildflower mixes within or adjacent to crop fields provide continuous floral resources across the growing season. Diverse pollinator communities (wild bees, hoverflies, butterflies) build up in these strips and service adjacent crops, increasing pollination quality and quantity. The structural diversity also supports natural enemy populations that reduce pest pressure.
interventions.effect_size: +5–20% crop yield from improved pollination; 12% increase in fruit set in orchards within 50 m; 25% reduction in misshapen fruit
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & Albrecht et al. (2020)
co_benefits: Yield and quality boost for insect-pollinated commercial crops
Landscape aesthetic enhancement
Spillover of predatory insects controlling aphids
trade_offs: Dedicated land allocation removed from direct crop harvest
Requires weed management during establishment year

interventions.name: Integrated Pest Management with biological controls
interventions.mechanism: IPM replaces broad-spectrum chemical pesticides with biological control agents (predatory insects, parasitoid wasps, microbial biopesticides), habitat management to support natural enemies, and targeted minimal chemical intervention as a last resort. Reduced pesticide load allows recovery of non-target invertebrate communities, rebuilding the food web base that supports higher trophic levels including insectivorous birds and bats.
interventions.effect_size: 50–70% reduction in pesticide use; 30% higher invertebrate species richness; 40% greater bird abundance compared to conventional management
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & Pretty & Bharucha (2015)
co_benefits: Elimination of chemical pesticide residue on harvested produce
Reduced health hazards for farm workers
Conservation of beneficial non-target organisms
trade_offs: Requires higher biological literacy and scouting discipline
Biological control agents may act slower than knockdown chemical sprays

interventions.name: Mixed native-species reforestation (framework species method)
interventions.mechanism: Planting 20–30 fast-growing, fruiting native tree species catalyses natural forest succession by attracting seed-dispersing birds and bats. The resulting multi-layered canopy structure creates diverse microhabitat niches (light gaps, deadwood, understorey) that support a far wider range of species than monoculture plantations. Carbon sequestration benefits from complementary resource use (light, water, nutrients) among diverse species.
interventions.effect_size: 50–80% of old-growth species richness recovered within 15–25 years; 10–30% higher carbon sequestration than monoculture plantations; 60–100 additional plant species recruited via natural dispersal within a decade
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Cross-Chapter Paper 1 (CCP1) & Chapter 18: Climate Resilient Development
co_benefits: Long-term timber and non-timber forest product harvesting potential
Watershed protection and regional rainfall stabilization
Restoration of indigenous biodiversity complexes
trade_offs: High initial sapling planting and sapling protection costs
Decadal return horizon before full ecosystem maturity

interventions.name: Contour bunding and rainwater harvesting micro-catchments
interventions.mechanism: Physical structures (contour stone bunds, zai pits, half-moon micro-catchments) capture and concentrate scarce rainfall at the root zone in semi-arid environments. By reducing surface runoff by 40–60%, they decrease downstream soil loss, increase soil moisture availability, and enable vegetation establishment on previously degraded, crusted soils. The concentrated water and nutrient inputs create productive microsites that gradually expand as vegetation recovers.
interventions.effect_size: 300–500% yield increase on degraded soils (zai pits); 40–60% runoff reduction; rehabilitation of 200,000–300,000 ha demonstrated in semi-arid zones
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia (Section 10.4.3) & Reij et al. (2009)
co_benefits: Restoration of barren agricultural lands to productive cultivation
Local shallow aquifer recharge
Substantial erosion prevention during flash rainstorms
trade_offs: Significant initial manual labor or earthmoving machinery required
Structures require seasonal repair following extreme storm runoff

interventions.name: Biochar soil amendment
interventions.mechanism: Pyrolysis of organic biomass at 300–700°C produces a highly stable, porous carbon structure that resists microbial decomposition for centuries. When incorporated into soil, biochar's high porosity increases water-holding capacity and provides habitat for beneficial microorganisms. Its alkaline nature raises soil pH in acidic soils, improving nutrient availability. The recalcitrant carbon structure means 70–80% of applied carbon remains after 100 years.
interventions.effect_size: +10–25% crop yield (greatest in acidic, sandy tropical soils); +15–20% soil water-holding capacity; pH increase of 0.2–1.0 units; 70–80% carbon persistence after 100 years
interventions.source: IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 10: Asia & IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land (SRCCL)
co_benefits: Century-scale stable soil carbon sequestration
Reduced nutrient leaching and improved fertilizer use efficiency
Amelioration of acidic soils without chemical lime
trade_offs: High upfront cost of biochar material and transport
Dust handling hazards and application logistics
